questions.question: Choose the correct indirect speech for the given sentence: She said to me, "I am going to Mumbai tomorrow."

options.text: She told me that she was going to Mumbai the next day.
options.explanation: 'said to' changes to 'told', 'I' changes to 'she' (referring to the speaker), 'am going' (present continuous) changes to 'was going' (past continuous), and 'tomorrow' changes to 'the next day' in indirect speech.

options.text: She said to me that she was going to Mumbai tomorrow.
options.explanation: Incorrect usage of 'said to' in indirect speech.

options.text: She told me that I was going to Mumbai the next day.
options.explanation: Incorrect pronoun usage, 'I' should be 'she'.

options.text: She said that she is going to Mumbai the next day.
options.explanation: Incorrect verb tense, 'is going' should be 'was going'.

questions.explanation: 'said to' changes to 'told', 'I' changes to 'she' (referring to the speaker), 'am going' (present continuous) changes to 'was going' (past continuous), and 'tomorrow' changes to 'the next day' in indirect speech.
questions.subject: upbo11-english

questions.question: Convert the following sentence into indirect speech: The teacher said, "The Earth revolves around the Sun."

options.text: The teacher said that the Earth revolved around the Sun.
options.explanation: Incorrect verb tense, 'revolves' is a universal truth and does not change.

options.text: The teacher told that the Earth revolves around the Sun.
options.explanation: Incorrect usage of 'told' without an object.

options.text: The teacher said that the Earth revolves around the Sun.
options.explanation: Universal truths, scientific facts, or habitual actions do not change their tense in indirect speech, even if the reporting verb is in the past tense.

options.text: The teacher said that the Earth had revolved around the Sun.
options.explanation: Incorrect verb tense, 'revolves' is a universal truth and does not change to 'had revolved'.

questions.explanation: Universal truths, scientific facts, or habitual actions do not change their tense in indirect speech, even if the reporting verb is in the past tense.
questions.subject: upbo11-english

questions.question: Select the correct indirect speech for the sentence: He said to me, "Are you coming to the party?"

options.text: He told me whether I am coming to the party.

options.text: He asked me if you were coming to the party.

questions.question: Change 'He says, "I am going to school."' into indirect speech.

options.text: He says that I am going to school.

options.text: He says that he is going to school.

options.explanation: The reporting verb is in the present tense, so the tense of the verb in the reported speech should not change.

questions.explanation: When the reporting verb is in the present tense ('says'), the tense of the verb in the reported speech does not change. Only pronouns change according to the subject of the reporting verb. 'I' changes to 'he'.

questions.question: Change 'The captain said to his soldiers, "March forward!"' into indirect speech.

options.text: The captain told his soldiers that they should march forward.
options.explanation: The reporting verb should change to 'ordered', and the sentence should be in the infinitive form, not 'that' clause.

questions.question: Change 'She said, "Alas! I am undone."' into indirect speech.

options.text: She exclaimed with joy that she was undone.
options.explanation: The emotion expressed is sorrow, not joy.

options.text: She said sadly that she was undone.
options.explanation: The sentence should start with 'exclaimed with sorrow' to convey the strong emotion.

options.text: She exclaimed with sorrow that she was undone.
options.explanation: The sentence starts with 'exclaimed with sorrow', and the tense changes to past simple.

options.text: She exclaimed that she had been undone.
options.explanation: The tense should change to past simple ('was'), not past perfect ('had been').

questions.explanation: Exclamatory sentences express strong emotions. 'Alas!' indicates sorrow, so 'exclaimed with sorrow' is appropriate. The sentence then changes to an assertive form, and the tense changes from present ('am') to past ('was').

questions.question: Change 'He said to me, "When will you return?"' into indirect speech.

options.text: He asked me when would I return.
options.explanation: The correct sentence structure is assertive, and 'when' acts as a conjunction.

options.text: He asked me when I would return.
options.explanation: The reporting verb changes to 'asked', 'when' acts as a conjunction, and the modal 'will' changes to 'would'.

options.text: He asked me that when I would return.
options.explanation: The correct conjunction is 'when', not 'that when'.

options.text: He asked me when you would return.
options.explanation: The pronoun 'you' should change to 'I' because it refers to 'me'.

questions.explanation: For 'wh-' interrogative sentences, the 'wh-' word (when) acts as the conjunction. The reporting verb 'said to' changes to 'asked'. The sentence structure becomes assertive, and the modal 'will' changes to 'would'. The pronoun 'you' changes to 'I' as it refers to 'me'.

questions.question: Change 'The old man said, "I must go now."' into indirect speech.

options.text: The old man said that he must go then.
options.explanation: The 'must' should change to 'had to' in indirect speech.

options.text: The old man said that he had to go now.
options.explanation: The adverb 'now' should change to 'then' in indirect speech.

options.text: The old man said that he had to go then.
options.explanation: The 'must' changes to 'had to', and the adverb 'now' changes to 'then'.

options.text: The old man said that he would go then.
options.explanation: The 'must' should change to 'had to', not 'would go'.

questions.question: Change 'The student said, "If I had studied harder, I would have passed the exam."' into indirect speech.

options.text: The student said that if he studied harder, he would pass the exam.
options.explanation: The condition is in the past perfect, and the consequence is in the conditional perfect; these tenses should remain unchanged.

options.text: The student said that if he had studied harder, he would pass the exam.
options.explanation: The condition and consequence tenses should remain unchanged as they are already in the past perfect and conditional perfect, respectively.

options.text: The student said that if he had studied harder, he would have passed the exam.
options.explanation: The tenses in the conditional sentence remain unchanged because they already refer to a past situation.

options.text: The student said that if he had studied harder, he would had passed the exam.
options.explanation: The correct form of the conditional perfect is 'would have passed', not 'would had passed'.

questions.explanation: This is a conditional sentence (Type 3) in the past perfect. Tenses in conditional clauses (especially Type 2 and 3) generally do not change in indirect speech if the condition remains unfulfilled or hypothetical, as it already refers to a past situation.
questions.subject: upbo11-english

questions.question: Change '"What a beautiful day!" exclaimed the tourist.' into indirect speech.

options.text: The tourist exclaimed that it was a beautiful day.

options.text: The tourist exclaimed that it was a very beautiful day.

options.text: The tourist exclaimed what a beautiful day it was.

options.text: The tourist exclaimed that it had been a beautiful day.

questions.explanation: Exclamatory sentences often use 'what' or 'how' without an explicit 'very'. In indirect speech, these are usually replaced by 'very' or 'great' to emphasize the degree. The exclamatory sentence is converted into an assertive sentence, and the tense changes from present ('is' implied) to past ('was').
